paragraphs: This paper investigates a safety problem that arises when language models handle multiple tasks concurrently. Most jailbreak approaches organize tasks sequentially, so the model encounters and answers them one after another. The authors instead introduce a word-level method in which neighboring words can belong to different intents, allowing tasks to be represented together.

Evaluations on mathematics and general question answering show that models retain strong usefulness under this concurrent arrangement. However, combining a harmful task with a benign one substantially lowers the probability that a guardrail filters it. The same ability to interpret intertwined tasks therefore creates a setting in which useful task performance and safety filtering can come apart.

The authors develop JAIL-CON, an iterative attack framework built around this finding. Experiments on widely used models report strong jailbreak performance relative to existing attacks. Its concurrent answers are also less detectable by the evaluated guardrail than previous attacks’ sequential answers. These findings identify task organization as a consequential factor in evaluating model safeguards.
neurips-2025-adjacent-words-divergent-in.tldr: JAIL-CON shows that concurrent task processing can preserve language-model usefulness while making harmful requests and responses harder for guardrails to detect.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what AI evaluations can tell us about behavior after deployment. Its central concern is that an AI system might understand the circumstances in which it is being tested and reason strategically about them. If that possibility matters, interpreting test results requires considering how the testing situation influences the behavior being observed.

The authors make two connected arguments. First, evaluations must account for possible strategic reasoning if they are to remain informative about deployment. Second, game theory can help formalize the reasoning used to turn evaluation results into safety claims. This offers a way to scrutinize the connection between observed test behavior and the conclusions drawn from it.

The paper supports these arguments through examples involving existing AI systems, a review of relevant research, and formal analysis of a simplified evaluation scenario. It also motivates further research directions. The claim is about accommodating a possible source of misleading evidence, rather than establishing that every AI system reasons strategically or that every evaluation is uninformative.
neurips-2025-ai-testing-should-account-f.tldr: This position paper argues that AI evaluations should account for possible strategic behavior and use game theory to examine evaluation-based safety claims.

paragraphs: Scientific machine learning often needs derivatives combined into partial differential equation operators. Computing these quantities through nested backpropagation is popular but expensive, which restricts their practical use. Forward differentiation approaches, including Taylor-mode automatic differentiation, offer another route. This paper improves how Taylor mode carries out the required derivative computations.

The proposed optimization rewrites the computational graph to collapse derivatives. Its essential modification is to propagate a sum through the graph. The authors show how this procedure applies to general linear partial differential equation operators and to randomized Taylor mode. The contribution therefore concerns the organization of derivative computation, with applications across these operator settings.

The authors implement the procedure and evaluate it on commonly used differential operators. Their results show faster Taylor-mode computation and better performance than nested backpropagation in those evaluations. They also argue that a machine learning compiler could perform the required graph changes, keeping the added complexity away from users. That compiler integration is presented as a possibility, while the implemented acceleration supplies the empirical evidence.
neurips-2025-collapsing-taylor-mode-auto.tldr: Rewriting computational graphs to collapse derivative calculations accelerates Taylor-mode differentiation for partial differential equation operators.

paragraphs: Tabular in-context learning faces a tradeoff between handling table structure efficiently and understanding what table contents mean. Architectures designed specifically for tables can use context effectively, but exclusive training on synthetic data limits their use of real-world semantics. Approaches built on pretrained language models bring semantic knowledge but can accommodate only limited context because of their architectures.

ConTextTab seeks to combine these strengths within a framework designed for tables. It uses specialized embeddings for different data modalities and trains on large-scale real-world tabular data. These choices integrate semantic understanding and alignment into the prediction framework, allowing the meaning carried by real data to contribute alongside its tabular organization.

Across a broad collection of benchmarks, the resulting model is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. It establishes a new leading result on CARTE, a benchmark with rich semantic content. The distinction matters: the abstract reports broad competitiveness and a particular strength on CARTE, rather than claiming superiority on every task. The findings support incorporating real-world semantics into table-native learning.
neurips-2025-contexttab-a-semantics-awar.tldr: ConTextTab combines table-native in-context learning with semantic representations and real-world training data, achieving competitive results and leading performance on CARTE.

paragraphs: A correct answer does not reveal whether a model found an insightful solution or worked through a much longer route. This paper introduces a benchmark of brainteasers written as extended narratives to examine that distinction. The puzzles permit different approaches, including short solutions built around a creative insight and longer solutions that rely more heavily on brute force.

The evaluation looks beyond correctness to the quality and creativity of solutions. It examines whether models can translate narrative puzzles into precise mathematical formulations, revise solutions using provided gold solutions, produce step-by-step solution sketches, and benefit from hints. Together, these activities expose different aspects of the problem-solving process rather than reducing it to a final-answer score.

The authors find that language models often produce creative and insightful solutions, suggesting that they possess some capacities relevant to novel problem solving. They also identify cases where models choose brute force despite an available, more efficient creative approach. The results therefore support a qualified picture of reasoning ability and identify solution strategy as a useful target for improvement.
neurips-2025-creativity-or-brute-force-u.tldr: A narrative-brainteaser benchmark finds that language models can produce insightful solutions but sometimes use brute force when a more creative route is available.

paragraphs: Controllers trained with reinforcement learning in simulation can lose substantial performance when deployed in the real world. DEAL addresses this reality gap through system identification: estimating physical parameters so that the simulator better matches the target environment. The paper focuses on difficulties that arise when many parameters must be identified, including inaccurate estimates and unstable convergence.

DEAL combines two mechanisms in an iterative process using limited real-world data. A discriminator evaluates how similar simulated state transitions are to transitions in the target environment, supplying fitness guidance. Diffusion evolution then adjusts noise prediction and denoising to improve the distribution of candidate physical parameters. These components jointly pursue closer agreement between simulated and target dynamics.

The authors evaluate the framework in both simulated and real-world environments. They report state-of-the-art identification accuracy and stability relative to the evaluated baselines on high-dimensional identification tasks, alongside substantial improvements in transfer to reality. The stated findings connect better parameter estimation with better controller deployment while emphasizing that the method requires only a small amount of real-world data.
neurips-2025-deal-diffusion-evolution-ad.tldr: DEAL combines adversarial feedback with diffusion evolution to estimate simulator parameters from limited real data and improve sim-to-real controller transfer.

paragraphs: Entropic regularization makes optimal transport problems easier to solve computationally, but it also shifts the answer away from the unregularized solution. Decreasing regularization as optimization progresses offers a way to benefit from the initial acceleration while reducing that bias. This paper gives theoretical support for that strategy in semi-discrete transport, where the source distribution is continuous and the target is discrete.

The authors introduce DRAG, a stochastic gradient algorithm that lowers regularization as the number of optimization steps grows and uses gradient averaging. Their analysis establishes that decreasing regularization can accelerate convergence compared with keeping it fixed. This turns a strategy previously used heuristically into one with explicit guarantees in the studied setting.

For the transport cost and potential estimates, the reported unbiased sample and iteration rate is O(1/t), where t indexes progress. For the transport map, the rate is O(1/sqrt(t)). These distinct rates describe different outputs of the transport problem. Numerical experiments support the analysis and demonstrate practical benefits, linking the theoretical reduction in regularization bias to observed solver performance.
neurips-2025-decreasing-entropic-regular.tldr: DRAG progressively reduces entropic regularization and provides convergence guarantees showing benefits over fixed regularization in semi-discrete optimal transport.

paragraphs: Large language models are costly to deploy because they demand substantial memory and computation. Pruning reduces those costs by removing weights, but many methods overlook the activation sparsity that appears during execution. DuoGPT combines these two sources of sparsity, treating sparse runtime activations as a form of dynamically structured sparsity in the weights.

The framework joins unstructured weight pruning with activation sparsity to create computations involving both sparse weights and sparse activations. To protect accuracy, the authors extend Optimal Brain Compression with calibration that accounts for activations. They also use output residuals from the original dense model as correction terms and optimize the resulting computation for GPUs and billion-parameter models.

Evaluations on LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 report accuracy improvements of up to 9.17% over state-of-the-art structured pruning methods when compared at the same 1.39× speedup over the dense baseline. This matched-speed comparison matters because it evaluates retained accuracy under a shared acceleration target. The result supports jointly designing pruning, calibration, and execution around both forms of sparsity.
neurips-2025-duogpt-training-free-dual-s.tldr: DuoGPT combines weight and activation sparsity with accuracy corrections and GPU optimization to improve the accuracy–speed tradeoff without training.

paragraphs: Large-scale language-model training depends on how GPUs exchange data as well as on their computing capacity. Communication occurs in high-volume bursts within particular groups of GPUs. When scheduling places those groups poorly across a data-center network, their traffic can compete for bandwidth and reduce training performance. This paper studies that scheduling problem at large scale.

The authors introduce Arnold, a scheduling system that aligns training communication patterns with physical network topology. They first characterize how the network’s physical organization affects pretraining jobs, then use those observations to design the scheduling algorithm. The approach makes the placement of communicating resources an explicit part of improving the training pipeline.

Simulation experiments show reductions in the maximum spread of communication groups by up to a factor of 1.67. In production training on more than 9,600 Hopper GPUs, Arnold improves end-to-end performance by 10.6%. These results provide evidence at two levels: the scheduler improves a property of group placement in simulation, and it delivers an overall training benefit in the reported production setting.
neurips-2025-efficient-pre-training-of-l.tldr: Arnold aligns GPU communication groups with data-center topology, improving end-to-end production training performance by 10.6% on more than 9,600 GPUs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning research depends on connecting training algorithms to environments in which agents act and learn. When those components use inconsistent interfaces, researchers face extra implementation work and have more difficulty comparing or extending one another’s results. Gymnasium addresses this infrastructure problem through an open-source library with a standard interface for reinforcement-learning environments.

Its central contribution is a set of abstractions that supports broad interoperability between environments and training algorithms. The library also supplies ready-to-use environments, tools for customizing them, and support for reproducibility and robustness. These pieces place environment interaction within a common framework while still allowing researchers to adapt environments to their own work.

The paper presents standardization as a practical means of streamlining algorithm development and testing. A shared interface reduces the implementation burden involved in assembling research components, leaving more attention for the algorithms themselves. The contribution is therefore reusable research infrastructure: it makes experiments easier to construct and build upon, with comparison and reproducibility as central motivations.
neurips-2025-gymnasium-a-standard-interf.tldr: Gymnasium standardizes reinforcement-learning environment interfaces and supplies tools that simplify experimentation, interoperability, and reproducibility.

paragraphs: Forecasting data that varies across locations and time requires recognizing both recurring patterns and departures from them. ST-SSDL focuses on the second part: differences between current observations and historical behavior can contain important predictive information. The framework explicitly connects each input to its historical average so that these deviations become part of the learning process.

It organizes the model’s hidden representations around learnable prototypes representing typical patterns across space and time. Two additional training objectives refine that organization. A contrastive objective makes different prototypes more distinguishable, while a deviation objective regularizes distance consistency between input representations and their corresponding prototypes. These objectives are trained jointly with the forecasting objective.

The design gives deviations a structured role in the hidden space, with the aim of improving generalization across differing input conditions. Experiments on six benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple metrics. Visualizations also show adaptive responses to different deviation levels. Together, the findings support explicitly learning how present conditions differ from historical patterns as part of forecasting.
neurips-2025-how-different-from-the-past.tldr: ST-SSDL improves spatio-temporal forecasting by organizing representations around typical patterns and explicitly learning deviations from historical behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies how gradient-based training learns a two-layer neural network with quadratic activations in high dimensions. It analyzes a structured data-generating model: inputs are Gaussian, signal directions are orthonormal, and the target combines second-Hermite-polynomial responses along those directions. This setting makes it possible to study learning dynamics with mathematical precision.

The number of signal directions grows as a power of input dimension, with an exponent between zero and one. Their nonnegative coefficients follow a power-law decay. Under these assumptions, the authors analyze stochastic gradient descent in the feature-learning regime, covering both a population limit and an online, finite-sample version. The analysis tracks learning rather than treating the features as fixed.

The resulting scaling laws describe power-law relationships between prediction risk and optimization time, sample size, and model width. The proof combines a detailed study of a matrix Riccati differential equation with matrix monotonicity arguments to establish convergence for the effective infinite-dimensional dynamics. These results explain resource–accuracy relationships within the specified quadratic model and its data assumptions.
neurips-2025-learning-quadratic-neural-n.tldr: The paper derives SGD dynamics and prediction-risk scaling laws for quadratic networks under a structured high-dimensional Gaussian data model.

paragraphs: Instruction fine-tuning helps pretrained language models follow requests and perform particular tasks, but producing high-quality training examples can be costly. MASTER addresses that data bottleneck by enriching existing examples through simulated teaching. Its central idea is to generate interactions among multiple agents representing different cognitive levels, making teaching conversations a source of additional training material.

The method uses three teaching scenarios grounded in pedagogy to produce teacher–student interaction data. Applying this process to existing datasets, including Orca-Math-200k, ProcQA, and OpenHermes2.5, yields the BOOST-QA fine-tuning dataset. The contribution links a conversational data-generation procedure with a concrete dataset built from material already available for training.

Models fine-tuned on BOOST-QA show strong performance across multiple benchmarks and strong generalization across tasks. The authors also report significant improvements in reasoning on complex tasks. These results support simulated teaching interactions as a useful form of data augmentation. The stated contribution concerns how training examples are enriched and the performance of models subsequently trained on them.
neurips-2025-master-enhancing-large-lang.tldr: MASTER generates simulated teacher–student conversations to enrich fine-tuning data, improving evaluated models’ multitask generalization and complex reasoning.

paragraphs: The brain can reorganize knowledge away from immediate interaction, using replay to consolidate memories, extract patterns, or simulate new situations. This paper asks how those different activities might be coordinated. It proposes a reinforcement-learning framework in which a meta-controller manages a lower-level learner during offline sleep phases to improve reward during later awake phases.

The meta-controller chooses among activities such as learning from recent memories, extracting patterns into a world model, and learning from generated data. It also learns to estimate the value of individual episodes. Those estimates support prioritizing both remembered experiences and newly generated simulations, making the selection of replay content part of the control problem.

Experiments involving image classification, maze solving, and relational inference show that the controller learns an adaptive curriculum for offline learning. The framework therefore connects decisions about what to replay with decisions about which kind of offline processing to perform. The authors present this as groundwork for normative neuroscience predictions about when particular replay strategies would be useful.
neurips-2025-modelling-the-control-of-of.tldr: A reinforcement-learning meta-controller learns which offline learning activities and replay episodes help a lower-level learner perform better later.

paragraphs: Maritime object detectors face limited annotated data and difficulty generalizing across object types, viewpoints, locations, and imaging conditions. Neptune-X addresses both problems through the training data. It combines synthetic scene generation with selection of examples that are relevant to the detection task, connecting the production of additional data to its usefulness for learning.

Its X-to-Maritime generator accepts conditioning from multiple modalities to create varied maritime scenes. A bidirectional attention module models interactions at the boundary between objects and water, aiming to improve visual realism where the two meet. An attribute-correlated active sampling method then dynamically chooses synthetic samples according to their relevance to the downstream task.

The authors also introduce the Maritime Generation Dataset to support generative learning across a broad range of semantic conditions. Experiments report leading maritime synthesis results and significant improvements in detection accuracy, especially in challenging or previously underrepresented settings. The findings support combining realistic generation with task-aware selection, so that expanding a training set also addresses gaps in the conditions it represents.
neurips-2025-neptune-x-active-x-to-marit.tldr: Neptune-X combines realistic maritime scene generation with task-aware sample selection to improve object detection, particularly in underrepresented conditions.

paragraphs: This paper provides a finite-time analysis of asynchronously implemented average-reward Q-learning. The algorithm uses adaptive step sizes that serve as separate local clocks for state–action pairs. These clocks account for the fact that different pairs receive updates at different times, making the treatment of asynchronous learning central to the result.

The authors establish a mean-square error rate of approximately O(1/k), up to logarithmic factors, measured using the span seminorm. For the algorithm studied, adaptive step sizes are necessary: without them, it fails to converge to the correct target. The paper interprets their effect as implicit importance sampling that compensates for the uneven influence of asynchronous updates.

Proving the rate is difficult because the adaptive step sizes depend on the full sample history and become strongly correlated with the current estimates. The authors reformulate this history-dependent stochastic approximation as a time-inhomogeneous Markovian process. They then combine time-varying bounds, conditioning, and Markov-chain concentration tools to control those correlations and establish the finite-time guarantee.
neurips-2025-non-asymptotic-guarantees-f.tldr: The paper proves a roughly O(1/k) finite-time error rate for asynchronous average-reward Q-learning and establishes the need for adaptive step sizes in the studied algorithm.

paragraphs: Masked discrete diffusion generates outputs by filling masked positions, but the models discussed here cannot revise a token once it has been generated. That prevents later steps from correcting an earlier mistake. ReMDM introduces a sampler that allows remasking, restoring a form of iterative refinement to this generation process.

The sampler is derived from a discrete diffusion model with a specially designed remasking backward process and can be applied to pretrained masked diffusion models. Increasing its sampling steps lets natural-language output quality approach that of autoregressive models. When computation is limited, the method also better preserves quality, making the sampling procedure a way to adjust the tradeoff between generation effort and output quality.

The reported benefits extend beyond language generation. ReMDM improves samples for discretized images and supports guidance in molecule design, advancing the controllability tradeoff relative to classical masking and uniform-noise diffusion. Applied to large pretrained diffusion language models, it also improves downstream tasks involving factual knowledge and reasoning. These findings connect revisable outputs with useful inference-time computation.
neurips-2025-remasking-discrete-diffusio.tldr: ReMDM lets pretrained masked diffusion models revise generated tokens, improving sample quality and enabling useful scaling with additional inference steps.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a general ReLU under Gaussian inputs when the labels need not be perfectly described by any ReLU. Performance is measured by squared error relative to the best-fitting ReLU, whose error is called opt. The goal is an efficient learner with error O(opt) plus an adjustable tolerance epsilon.

The authors show that black-box access to label queries can substantially reduce the number of labels required. Their computationally efficient algorithm uses a query count consisting of d times a polylogarithmic function of 1/epsilon, plus a term that is roughly the smaller of 1/p and 1/epsilon. Here d is the dimension, and p is the target function’s bias parameter.

They also prove that the query bound is qualitatively close to optimal, even without computational restrictions. A separate lower bound distinguishes this access from selecting labels out of an unlabeled pool: pool-based active learners require roughly d/epsilon labels unless they draw super-polynomially many unlabeled examples. The findings make the form of interaction a decisive part of label efficiency.
neurips-2025-robust-regression-of-genera.tldr: Black-box label queries enable efficient robust learning of general ReLUs with near-optimal query complexity, exceeding what ordinary pool-based active learning can achieve.

paragraphs: STSBench evaluates whether vision-language models understand driving situations across space and time. It automatically identifies predefined traffic scenarios using a dataset’s ground-truth annotations, offers an interface for human verification, and generates multiple-choice questions. The framework turns annotated driving data into scenario-based tests of reasoning about traffic behavior.

Applying the framework to nuScenes produces STSnu, with 43 scenarios and 971 human-verified questions spanning multiple views and frames. It targets expert models for end-to-end driving that process multi-camera video or LiDAR. Its questions assess reasoning about the ego vehicle’s actions and interactions among traffic participants, extending evaluation beyond semantic tasks such as recognizing or describing objects.

The evaluation uncovers substantial weaknesses in existing models’ understanding of fundamental traffic dynamics in complex environments. The authors argue that these findings motivate architectures that explicitly model spatial and temporal reasoning. The benchmark’s contribution is to make those abilities directly assessable using comprehensive three-dimensional perception, providing a basis for developing driving models with more robust and explainable behavior.
neurips-2025-stsbench-a-spatio-temporal-.tldr: STSBench creates verified driving-scenario questions that expose weaknesses in vision-language models’ reasoning about traffic across views and time.

paragraphs: Low-rank optimization reduces the memory needed to train language models, but memory savings alone do not ensure fast convergence. This paper focuses on optimization landscapes whose behavior differs sharply across directions. Standard isotropic steepest-descent methods can perform poorly in these settings, motivating update rules that account more explicitly for the landscape’s spectral structure.

SUMO performs exact singular value decomposition to orthogonalize optimization moments inside a low-dimensional subspace that adapts during training. This enables norm-inducing steepest-descent updates while avoiding approximation errors associated with methods such as Newton–Schulz orthogonalization. The authors derive an upper bound linking those errors to moment condition numbers and analytically show that relevant conditions occur during language-model training.

The paper presents theoretical and empirical evidence that exact orthogonalization through SVD improves convergence rates while reducing overall complexity. Evaluations also report better stability and performance, with memory reductions of up to 20% relative to state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is the combination of exact orthogonalization and an adaptive low-dimensional working space to improve both optimization and memory use.
neurips-2025-sumo-subspace-aware-moment-.tldr: SUMO uses exact moment orthogonalization in an adaptive low-dimensional subspace to accelerate language-model training and reduce memory use.

paragraphs: Evaluating coding models on real bug fixes requires both representative issues and executable environments for checking proposed patches. The paper identifies three constraints in SWE-bench: a static task collection, coverage limited to 12 repositories, and substantial manual work in creating instances and environments. SWE-bench-Live addresses these constraints with a benchmark designed for continuing updates.

The reported collection contains 1,890 tasks drawn from GitHub issues created since 2024 across 223 repositories. Every task has a dedicated Docker image to support reproducible execution. An automated curation pipeline handles the process from constructing an instance through setting up its environment, reducing the manual bottlenecks that previously restricted expansion.

The authors evaluate a range of state-of-the-art models and agent frameworks on this collection to examine practical bug-fixing capability. The main contribution is a broader, executable evaluation resource paired with a process for keeping it fresh. Combining repository diversity, reproducible task environments, and ongoing curation supports large-scale assessment grounded in real development activity.
neurips-2025-swe-bench-goes-live-7e4cb70.tldr: SWE-bench-Live automates curation of reproducible bug-fixing tasks across hundreds of repositories to support continuously updated coding-agent evaluation.

paragraphs: Neural-network fingerprinting embeds ownership information in a model, but that information needs to survive subsequent changes to remain useful. This paper develops a fingerprinting method with a theoretical robustness result for fine-tuning. Its design focuses on specific frequency components of convolutional filters that can remain unchanged during gradient-descent updates.

The guarantee has an explicit condition: the input features of the convolutional layer contain only low-frequency components. Under that condition, the authors prove that particular filter frequency components are unaffected by gradient descent during fine-tuning. They introduce a revised Fourier transform to extract those components and use them as the location for embedded fingerprint information.

The authors additionally prove equivariance to weight scaling and weight permutations, meaning that the relevant components transform in a corresponding way under those operations. A fingerprint module puts the theoretical construction into practice, and preliminary experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The result supplies a mathematically motivated place to store ownership information, with fine-tuning robustness tied to the stated condition on layer inputs.
neurips-2025-towards-the-resistance-of-n.tldr: The paper embeds ownership fingerprints in convolutional-filter frequency components proven stable under fine-tuning when layer inputs contain only low frequencies.

paragraphs: CLIP learns to align images and text from large collections of paired web data. That dependence on uncurated data creates opportunities for poisoning and backdoors. ToxicTextCLIP investigates the text side of this vulnerability, which has received less attention than image-based attacks, and targets the pretraining stage of vision-language learning.

The framework addresses two related difficulties: text backgrounds can be semantically inconsistent with a target class, and suitable background-consistent texts can be scarce. It iteratively combines a selector that prioritizes compatible background content with an augmenter that produces diverse, semantically coherent poisoned text. The approach treats background consistency as a central factor in constructing adversarial training material.

Experiments on classification and retrieval report poisoning success of up to 95.83% and backdoor Hit@1 of up to 98.68%. The framework also bypasses RoCLIP, CleanCLIP, and SafeCLIP in the reported evaluations. These results demonstrate a substantial text-modality attack surface in the studied settings and show that the evaluated defenses do not eliminate the risk posed by this framework.
neurips-2025-toxictextclip-text-based-po.tldr: ToxicTextCLIP demonstrates effective text-based poisoning and backdoor attacks on CLIP pretraining, including against three evaluated defenses.

paragraphs: Public repositories contain millions of models, yet incomplete documentation makes many difficult to understand or reuse. Their capabilities, origins, and constraints may be unclear, contributing to wasted computation, hidden biases, and intellectual-property risks. This position paper proposes a Model Atlas to organize that population and make relationships among models more accessible.

The atlas would be a graph containing models, their attributes, and the weight transformations that connect them. Such a structure could support model discovery, forensic analysis, and research that studies models themselves. However, building the graph also requires dealing with missing information, since undocumented models leave large portions of the proposed atlas unknown.

The authors call for methods that infer functionality, performance, and lineage directly from model weights. They argue that a scalable approach should bypass the parameter symmetries that complicate reasoning about weights. The paper presents a research agenda and community project: organizing model relationships and learning missing properties are complementary parts of making the existing model population more useful.
neurips-2025-we-should-chart-an-atlas-of.tldr: This position paper proposes a graph-based Model Atlas and methods for inferring undocumented models’ properties and lineage from their weights.

paragraphs: Latent action models compress changes between video frames into hidden representations intended to capture action-relevant information. The difficulty is that frame differences also include changes caused by external noise. This paper asks when the learned representation captures controllable changes and when it instead reflects variation unrelated to an agent’s actions.

The authors build a tractable linear model that captures the central learning problem. Their analysis connects latent action learning to principal component analysis and identifies desirable properties of the policy that generates the data. These connections help explain why the structure of the observed variation and the way actions are collected matter for what the representation learns.

The analysis also provides justification for strategies intended to favor controllable changes, including data augmentation, data cleaning, and auxiliary action prediction. Numerical simulations illustrate how the structure of observations, actions, and noise influences learning. The contribution is an analytical account supported by illustrative simulations, giving a basis for reasoning about action relevance within the studied linear setting.
neurips-2025-what-do-latent-action-model.tldr: A tractable linear analysis explains how latent action models can capture controllable changes or irrelevant noise and motivates strategies to favor action-relevant learning.
